http://www.euronews.com/2026/07/30/china.text: China has lodged an official complaint after New Zealand's foreign minister Winston Peters told a Chinese-born MP to "go back to your own country" during a heated parliamentary exchange in Wellington.Peters, the leader of the NZ First party, made the remarks on Wednesday after Green Party MP Lawrence Xu-Nan asked him, "Are you vaccinated?" during a debate over New Zealand's response to the Covid-19 pandemic.Xu-Nan was born in Tianjin, China, but grew up in New Zealand.Peters responded that the lawmaker had "come here five minutes ago" before telling him: "Go back to your own country.""This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to. Go back to where you've come from, you loudmouth," Peters added.Speaking to the 1News channel on Thursday, Xu-nan said: "It's a little bit unbelievable to have a Minister for Foreign Affairs, I guess, scapegoating the migrant communities as a distraction to shift the blame away from all of the harm that this government is doing."China lodges complaintThe remarks prompted a rare intervention from China's ambassador to New Zealand, Wang Xiaolong, who wrote on X that he normally avoided commenting on domestic politics but that "sometimes, a statement says more about the person that makes it than anything or anybody else".The Chinese embassy in Wellington said on Thursday it had lodged a complaint with New Zealand's foreign ministry over what it described as "negative China-related remarks made by a certain politician".Peters has refused to back down, arguing his comments were a defence of democratic freedoms."We live in a democracy that includes free speech and rights," he wrote on X, adding that he would "not resile from that point".New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, whose National Party governs in coalition with NZ First, condemned Peters' remarks as "inappropriate attention-seeking".NZ First politicians have faced criticism over similar remarks before. Last year, Peters' deputy Shane Jones shouted "send the Mexicans home" at MP Francisco Hernandez, who was born in the Philippines.Mexico's ambassador, Alfredo Pérez Bravo, subsequently issued an official diplomatic communication to New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, opting to raise the issue through diplomatic channels rather than publicly.Peters later withdrew his support for Jones' remarks, acknowledging that "in the heat of the moment" they "may have been expressed differently."

https://english.pravda.ru/news/hotspots/.text: Explosion Rocks Cargo Ship Bound for Ukraine Off Romaniaâs Coast 24.07.2026 13:58 Incidents A cargo vessel traveling from the United States to Ukraine under the Liberian flag suffered an explosion while sailing off the Romanian coast, according to Romania's Ministry of Internal Affairs. Romanian officials said the blast occurred overnight near cargo hold No. 6 aboard the Christiana B . According to the ministry's preliminary assessment, the explosion may have resulted from either a naval drone strike or the detonation of a sea mine. The Christiana B is a bulk carrier transporting coal from the U. S. port of Norfolk to Ukraine. Following the explosion, the crew issued a distress call. Authorities confirmed that no injuries were reported among those on board. Romanian authorities have launched an investigation into the incident to determine the exact cause of the explosion. The event comes shortly after a Romanian Air Force F-16 fighter jet intercepted and shot down an unidentified drone that had entered the country's airspace, highlighting ongoing security concerns in the Black Sea region. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: Vilnius: Stepping into the newly renovated Vilnius airport, visitors are greeted with a slew of billboards advertising products Made in Lithuania , including cybersecurity giant NordVPN.Rather than focusing on heritage or artisanal craftsmanship promoted in similar campaigns in Italy or France, Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours Estonia and Latvia are highlighting they are home to innovation.The three countries have a growing number of startups recognised worldwide, such as online reselling platform Vinted, rideshare service Bolt and videotelephony pioneer Skype.Despite a total population of just over six million people, the Baltic states possessed around 33,000 startups last year, according to data from Lursoft IT, a Latvian company specialising in business and financial databases.They raised 20 percent more in funding in 2025 at 607 million euros ($700 million), according to Practica Capital and Firstpick's annual report on the sector.The Baltic states now have 17 unicorns -- startups with a valuation above $1.0 billion. 'Entrepreneurial spirit' Fewer than four decades ago Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania regained their independence but inherited inefficient factories from the Soviet Union's command economy. Regaining independence... unlocked the entrepreneurial spirit previously suppressed under Soviet rule, said Latvian-American entrepreneur Girts Graudins, who noted that the region has a history as a science and manufacturing hub going back to the turn of the 20th century.The ruins of the Soviet command economy were also a crucible for innovation, said Kadri Ukrainski, who lectures on the subject at Estonia's Tartu University. Coming from (the) Soviet times, we didn't have very good telephone systems, she said, leading to the creation of Skype -- Estonia's first, and arguably its most famous, unicorn.The app helped the once-behind country leap forward, she argued, helping us to solve this very backward communication system .Founded in 2003 by a couple of Scandinavian entrepreneurs along with four Estonian developers, Skype had 50 million registered users worldwide by 2005, when it was sold to online auction site eBay for approximately $2.6 billion.European Union accession in 2004 also brought the Baltic states access to European markets.Estonia, with a population of 1.3 million, now has 10 active unicorns -- the most per capita in Europe. Startup 'multiplier effect' Although Skype is now defunct -- retired last year by Microsoft which bought the app in 2011, its legacy as the first Baltic unicorn can still be felt across the region.Known as the Skype mafia effect, founders and early employees took the experience they gained from the company and went on to start their own companies, inspiring others to do the same.Lithuania's first unicorn, second-hand clothing platform Vinted, has had a similar impact. Vinted's journey has certainly been intertwined with the broader development of Lithuania's startup ecosystem, said the company's vice president for corporate affairs, Jessie de la Merced, arguing that its presence has had a multiplier effect .Vinted, which became a unicorn in 2019, reached $8 billion in market valuation in April, and Lithuania now boasts a total of six unicorns.Unicorns' effects can also be felt across the local economy, said Karolina Urbonaite, the head of Startup Lithuania, a government institution which supports the country's startup ecosystem. Our startups pay a lot of taxes. They create new jobs, she said, adding that Lithuanian startups employed over 20,000 people in total, paying high salaries and attracting foreign investment to the country.A heavy focus on STEM education (Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics) in the Baltics is also helping forge the next generation of fintech entrepreneurs.Baltic STEM students rank higher than those from France, Sweden, the United States and Norway in the OECD's latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA).There has also been a change of aspirations. Before, the role models were artists and musicians, said Ronny Eriksson, founder of entrepreneurship studio New Nordic Way in Finland. But now it's actually startup people and you want to become those when you grow up .

https://www.budapesttimes.hu/books/polis.text: The Budapest Times “Stealing Hitler's Rocket: The Incredible Mission to Smuggle a V-2 Rocket Out of Nazi-Occupied Europe to Britain” by Guy Walters (published by Head of Zeus) Polish courage helped counter Germany’s last gasp Written by Christopher Osterberg By winter 1943-1944 the Third Reich’s goal of world domination was slipping away. The Eastern Front was collapsing westwards, Italy had become a ruinous stalemate and Allied bombers were unleashing freely over the Ruhr. But Adolf Hitler kept faith that his covert V-1 and V-2 rockets, his “Vengeance weapons”, would head off the looming catastrophe. The rockets were being developed by an extraordinary concentration of scientific talent: aerodynamicists, mathematicians, metallurgists, guidance experts and engineers of every type at remote Peenemünde on Germany’s Baltic coast. When Hitler visited in early 1944 to watch a V-2 test launch he pronounced it as a symbol of the Reich’s imminent resurgence. No one dared contradict the Führer. The V-2, or Vergeltungswaffe Zwei (Vengeance weapon two), in particular, author Guy Walters writes, was planned to be “a weapon so advanced that it seemed to belong to a future age, a ballistic missile capable of soaring beyond the atmosphere and then falling upon its earthly target at supersonic speed”. Hitler had become increasingly hopeful that his mighty rockets would blast Britain into submission. Civilian morale would collapse under the suddenness and terror of the strikes. The V-2 was the newer and more terrifying of the two weapons, as tall as a four-storey building and with a range of at least 320 kilometres. It would be the world’s first man-made object to reach space, then fall faster than the speed of sound and thus silently, invisibly, to bring London to its knees, the city’s spirit broken by attacks no one could predict or stop. But in occupied Poland the resistance was trying to find out the V-2’s secrets and get them to Britain. Guy Walters tells this gripping tale, a welcome addition to the history of World War Two, something newer and better than the retreads of chestnuts such as Dunkirk, the Blitz, Stalingrad, D-Day and others, even if they be refreshed by “new archives, diaries” and so on. More than 6000 people were living or working at Peenemünde. The German air force, the Luftwaffe, was working on the smaller, cheaper and simpler V-1, and Wernher von Braun, a visionary rocket engineer and scientist, was heading development of the V-2. Snippets of information began to reach London, where every scrap was gathered – aerial photos of long sheds, launch ramps, scorched sand, intercepted communications, overheard conversation. By late 1943 the Allies had become increasingly aware of Germany’s plan for a long-range, liquid oxygen-powered missile, and on August 17-18 the Royal Air Force launched Operation Hydra, destructive bombing raids that forced the V-1 and V-2 trials to be relocated to a more covert location, in remote forests near Blizna in occupied Poland. The Germans did not foresee that this put their most prized secret within reach of one of the most effective resistance networks in Europe, the Polish underground known as the Armia Krajowa (Home Army). The resistance was already deeply embedded throughout the region and, as had happened at Peenemünde, notice was made of the sudden increase in rail shipments, unusual vehicles and the cordoning off of wooded clearings. The first test launches left orange trails arcing across the Polish sky, then distant detonations. Here was something far more advanced than conventional artillery. To assess the scale of the Reich’s ballistic missile programme, Poles shadowed German recovery teams, mapped crash sites and retrieved bits and pieces, spiriting away debris before the Germans arrived. Reports by eyewitnesses, sketches, rumours from forced labourers and so on passed through clandestine channels to London. Missile fragments – shreds of wire, shards of metal, unidentifiable pieces of fittings, guidance vanes – reached Britain for analysts to determine their materials, make measurements and study the construction. By early 1944 the British were deeply worried as it became clear that the Nazis were close to having a supersonic weapon beyond interception. Operation Hydra had only delayed matters by a couple of months or so. Then, on May 20, 1944, a V-2 rocket crashed virtually intact near Sarnaki in Poland and the Home Army rushed to get there before the Germans. This was the bonanza for which the Allies had waited. Notes and drawings of the crashed V-2 reached Warsaw on July 5, 1944 and five days later the intelligence people in London requested that the full rocket be smuggled by aircraft to England. V-2 sections were dismantled and hidden under straw and timber in a barn. Then, in a highly dangerous operation the rocket was concealed in large oxygen cylinders welded shut with lead solder. Hitler’s “wonder weapon” was moved 240 kilometres by lorry across occupied Poland, using forged documentation from a fake oxygen works in Warsaw. The Home Army managed to get the V-2 to Motyl on July 15, 1944 and prepared a landing strip in a field, lit by lanterns. A tense wait among nearby Germans ensued until July 25-26 when a Dakota of the Royal Air Force 267 Squadron in Brindisi, southern Italy, arrived. The Dakota had flown 2500 kilometres across the Adriatic to the Dalmatian coast then through enemy airspace via Yugoslavia, Hungary, Slovakia and Poland to collect the V-2. It was a hazardous venture – of aircraft that had attempted the run from Brindisi to Europe, barely half returned. Then the plane had trouble taking off from the muddy Motyl field. Guy Walters: “It would remain one of the most extraordinary feats of the underground war: a nation under occupation delivering to its allies the very weapon meant for their destruction.” The smuggled V-2 reached England on July 27 and experts fell upon it. The author relates how V-1s, the world’s first rocket-delivered warhead, first began striking England on June 13, 1944, one week after the D-Day invasion of Normandy. When one hit a chapel in Wellington Barracks in central London on June 18 it left 262 people dead or injured. The “doodlebugs”, as they were known, were occasionally shot down by anti-aircraft guns or fighter planes, or caught up in barrage balloons. Improved radar tracking, tighter gun belts along the English coast and skilled pilots tipping them off course meant that well over half were being destroyed before reaching London. But they killed thousands of British people. On June 16, 1944, 405 Lancasters, Halifaxes and Mosquitos bombed four V-1 emplacements and further strikes followed. Advancing Allied forces eventually captured their launch sites and halted the weapon in its tracks, ending the terror but putting pressure on Hitler’s forces that was more acute than ever. V-2s were needed in quantity to redress German reversals. Hitler wanted London flattened, in revenge for Allied bombing on major German cities. “In fact,” writes Walters, “the V-2 was more likely to cause a collapse in morale, rather than wholesale destruction, but that would be enough, its avocates hoped, to change the course of the war.” And thus, “after years of improvisation, rivalry, and feverish engineering, Germany’s flying bomb entered the war – not as a miracle weapon, but as the product of desperation, industry, and the grim resolve of a Reich already sliding toward retreat.” A total 1190 V-2s hit England, the first on September 8, 1944 and the last on March 27, 1945. A strike on Woolworths at New Cross, London, killed 168 people in a single blow. The V-2s caused some 2700 deaths and 6500 serious injuries but could not save Hitler from defeat. Guy Walters, a British author, historian and journalist, offers this previously neglected story of the V-2’s origins, its designers, the awful conditions endured by concentration camp inmates to build it, the courage of the Poles and the British scramble to unlock its secrets. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/thomas-tu.text: Arthur Ferridge Tue, September 29, 2026 at 10:16 PM UTC 0 Thomas Tuchel did not go out of his way to look after Elliot Anderson and Marc Guehi after Manchester City were found guilty of serious financial misconduct by the Premier League , a move which he said has left him with “a bad conscience”. The Premier League confirmed their verdict and released a formal legal decision shortly before England’s Nations League clash with the Czech Republic kicked off on Tuesday night. Sanctions are yet to be confirmed, but City could be facing enforced relegation, expulsion from the Premier League, or considerable points deductions. Tuchel, though, persisted in handing City players Guehi and Anderson starts in Prague, though their team-mate Nico O’Reilly missed out through injury. Speaking after recording a 2-0 win , Tuchel admitted he should have checked in with them beforehand. “I have a bad conscience now,” he told BBC Radio 5 Live. “I did not actually because I am just focused on everything we have to deal with here and to prepare the team. “I did not talk to them about the issue and I will not comment on it. I think Marc today was absolutely excellent after a tough match against Spain. The reaction was on the highest level and Elliot Anderson had a good match as well.” Tuchel would not be goaded, either, into revealing whether he planned to rotate his side for Saturday’s match against Croatia, though he did lift the lid on England’s travel plans. He confirmed the Three Lions would head straight to a training camp in Croatia from Prague, rather than heading back to England first. “I cannot tell you (if we will rotate vs Croatia),” he continued. “We have three days which is a big difference to two games. We decided not to travel back to England but to stay in Prague one more night, get some good rest and then travel to Croatia and have two training sessions there. “We will push everyone to be available, even Nico O'Reilly and Ezri Konsa hopefully and then we know more. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck30.text: Image caption, Harryville principal Neil McCullough said pupils were afraid By Catherine Doyle BBC News NI Published 16 October 2026 The principal of a school that lost almost a fifth of its pupils in the wake of rioting in Ballymena has said staff found themselves in a "completely unprecedented situation". A report into the effect of the "racially motivated" disorder on young people has found that schools including Harryville Primary School were seen as a safe haven for children whose homes were under attack. However, it also found that 41 pupils from migrant families did not return to the school, which had to arrange hotel accommodation for some who were afraid to return home. Principal Neil McCullough said some families slept in cars due to the fear of what was happening on the streets. The rioting broke out after a planned peaceful protest, in response to an alleged serious sexual assault in the County Antrim town. Attempted rape charges against two Romanian teenagers were withdrawn in November 2025 by the Public Prosecution Service. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, PSNI officers in riot gear on a third night of civil unrest on 11 June 2025 in Ballymena Harryville's roll fell from 235 pupils on the first day of the riots to 120 the next day, with 41 children never returning. The principal described "the fear" of seeing what the children were going through. "We were seeing the houses of our pupils being attacked, protests outside houses," McCullough said. He added that families "turned up" the next morning at the school after the first night of disorder because they knew that was a "safe space". "They didn't have anywhere else to go with the prospect of having nowhere to go again that evening, nowhere to stay, some of them had slept in their cars in car parks the night before due to the fear of what was happening on their streets." 'Fear from walking the streets' Speaking on Evening Extra , he said the school did all it could "to protect them in any way we could" and had to help "find housing for them that night". "Children weren't getting to bed due to what was happening on the streets, due to sirens, due to the noise. "Children were coming into school having not slept the night before, children were coming into school with fear from walking the streets, even coming to school. "That took a heavy toll on our staff because they were carrying that burden and being cheery and upbeat and using our trauma-informed approach to try to look after those children." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Crowds clashed with police in Ballymena in June 2025 McCullough describes a new report into what happened as showing "the power of relationships within community". Meeting, Mapping, Moving - Ballymena Recovering , external looks at the "harrowing" impact the rioting had on people, particularly on children, young people and minority communities. McCullough said it builds on the "incredible work that's going on in Ballymena". "It's a report really focused on people and the power people can have to make a change whenever there is a shared vision and a shared goal," he said. 'Institutional unpreparedness' The report looked at a consultation by the Inter Ethnic Forum community, which conducted interviews with people from minority communities about how their lives were "disrupted". "Respondents described the terror of that night and the chaos that followed, with no clear pathway to safety and support arriving late or not at all for many families," the report states. One of the "system failures" identified by participants was that the Education Authority (EA) "failed to provide guidance or support" to Harryville PS, and left the school to "make impossible decisions alone". It said the EA told the school that families needed to leave the building by 18:00 BST, because of statutory restrictions but "given no alternative". "The school ultimately paid for hotel accommodation from its own budget. This is a damning indictment of institutional unpreparedness," the report added. McCullough said the EA "did what they could" in an unprecedented set of circumstances, adding people from the EA "did contact me and tried to offer what support they could". "None of us are perfect and we, as a school, didn't get it perfect either," he said. In a statement, the EA said it "made a range of support available" to schools in the area during the disorder, including Harryville. It said it supported pupils, families and staff, and organised activities and programmes afterwards. "We continue to work with schools, families, communities and statutory partners to ensure children feel safe, supported and able to learn." Image caption, Kim Carson, from Bytes project, worked with some of the young people involved in the unrest Youth worker Kim Carson, from Bytes, talked about the work she's been doing with some of the young people who were involved in the unrest. "They just felt very angered and frustrated, she said, adding: "A lot of them took their frustrations out in the wrong way." She said after the disorder there was "a lot of difficult conversations" with the young people. She added it was important to provide them with a "safe space" but to also "challenge what their thoughts were and give them other perspectives". 'Local knowledge' Lisa Mooney from Radius Housing, who helped bring the report together, said the "trauma" of what happened in June 2025 is still being felt in Ballymena. "It's had a huge and devastating impact on children and young people," she said. She said she hopes there is no more unrest but says one of the questions the report wants to answer is "what do we need to do" to make the community more ready if something does happen? She added it was important that grassroots work goes into planning how to deal with any future unrest by "listening to the community in terms of watching for a rise in tensions". "So creating a system where you're using local knowledge to identify tension early," she said. "A lot of this is about building and maintaining the relationships and continuing to do that."
